questions.question: Every day a vast amount of water, most of it from the oceans, turns into an invisible gas and rises into the air. Where does nearly all the energy for this change come from?
choices: Heat from the Sun
Heat from deep inside Earth
The pull of the Moon
The pull of Earth's gravity
questions.context: Sunlight warms the oceans, lakes and land, and its heat turns liquid water into water vapour; this change is evaporation. The heat rising from deep inside Earth is less than a thousandth as much as the Sun's. Gravity has the opposite job: it pulls rain and snow down and makes rivers run downhill.
questions.grade_note: Texas TEKS 5.10A has 5th graders explain how the Sun and the ocean interact in the water cycle, and Florida's grade 5 lessons (SC.5.E.7.1) teach that the Sun's heat provides the energy to evaporate water.

questions.question: After a summer shower, rain leaves a shallow puddle on a glass garden table. By late afternoon the sunshine has dried the table completely. Where did the water go?
questions.answer: Into the air as water vapour
choices: Into the air as water vapour
Through the glass into the ground
Up to the Sun, drawn by its heat
Nowhere, since it no longer exists
questions.context: The Sun's heat turned the puddle into water vapour, an invisible gas that mixed into the air; this is evaporation. The water still exists, and glass lets no water through, so none of it soaked away. In time that vapour may become part of a cloud.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 water-cycle lessons (SC.5.E.7.1) teach evaporation as liquid water changing to water vapour, and children's ideas that evaporated water 'disappeared', 'leaked through' its dish or that 'the sun took it away' are documented (SPACE project, via NZCER).

questions.question: Warm, damp air rises from the sea and cools as it climbs. High in the sky its water vapour turns back into tiny drops of liquid water, and the drops gather into clouds. What is this step of the water cycle called?
choices: Condensation
Evaporation
Precipitation
Transpiration
questions.context: Condensation is water vapour turning back into liquid water as it cools. Air cools as it rises, and its vapour condenses into droplets far too small and light to fall, which together make a cloud. Evaporation is the opposite change, and transpiration is water evaporating from the leaves of plants.
questions.grade_note: Water vapour cooling and condensing into the droplets that form clouds is one of the named parts of Florida's grade 5 water-cycle model (SC.5.E.7.1).

questions.question: Rain, snow, sleet and hail all fall from clouds, and together they are called precipitation. What makes rain begin to fall from a cloud?
questions.answer: Its tiny drops join into heavy drops
choices: Its tiny drops join into heavy drops
Two clouds bump into each other
The wind squeezes it like a sponge
It rips open like a bag of water
questions.context: A cloud is a crowd of droplets so small that rising air holds them up. When droplets bump and join, a drop grows until it is too heavy to stay up and falls as rain; it takes millions of cloud droplets to make one raindrop. A cloud is not a bag or a sponge full of water.
questions.grade_note: Rain falling from clouds is part of every grade 5 water-cycle model (Florida SC.5.E.7.1), and children's pictures of clouds as bags that rip open when they collide, or as sponges, are documented up to age 10 (Bar, in NSTA's summary).

questions.question: A heavy storm pours rain onto a hillside faster than the soil can soak it up. The extra water flows downhill across the land into creeks and rivers. What is this water called?
choices: Runoff
Groundwater
Meltwater
Spring water
questions.context: Runoff is rain or melted snow that flows over the land instead of soaking in. Creeks and rivers carry it downhill to lakes and the sea, where it collects. Water that soaks into the soil becomes groundwater, and spring water is groundwater flowing back out of the ground.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 lessons follow fallen rain back to the sea, with rivers returning runoff to the ocean (SC.5.E.7.2), and the USGS water cycle for schools names runoff as the water that reaches creeks, rivers, lakes and the oceans.

questions.question: After a long, gentle rain, some of the water soaks down through the soil of a meadow and becomes groundwater, deep under the land. What happens to groundwater over time?
questions.answer: It seeps slowly into rivers and seas
choices: It seeps slowly into rivers and seas
It stays in one place for ever
It slowly hardens into solid rock
It sinks to Earth's hot centre
questions.context: Groundwater moves slowly, often only centimetres to metres in a year. It seeps sideways and upwards into the beds of rivers, lakes and the sea, and flows out at springs, so it rejoins the rest of the water cycle. Deep groundwater may stay underground for thousands of years first.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-ESS2-2 names ground water among the reservoirs 5th graders study, and Florida's grade 5 lessons call the ground a large store of fresh water; the USGS water cycle for schools teaches that it seeps back into rivers, lakes and the oceans.

questions.question: Rain has fallen on Earth for millions of years, since long before the dinosaurs. How much water does Earth have today, compared with the dinosaurs' time?
questions.answer: About the same, used over and over
choices: About the same, used over and over
Less, since the Sun burns it up
More, since clouds make new water
Less, since the ground soaks it up
questions.context: The water cycle moves water from place to place and from one form to another, but Earth as a whole neither gains nor loses much water. Water that evaporates is still in the air, and water that soaks into the ground is still on Earth. The rain falling today is the same water that has gone round for millions of years.
questions.grade_note: Florida's grade 5 benchmark SC.5.E.7.1 teaches that water 'can go back and forth from one state to another', and the same water moving round the cycle again and again is the idea every 5th-grade water-cycle model is built on.

questions.question: Oceans cover about 71 percent of Earth's surface, and their water is salty. How much of all the water on Earth is in the oceans?
choices: Nearly all of it
About three quarters of it
About half of it
Only a small part of it
questions.context: About 97 percent of Earth's water is salty ocean water. Oceans cover less of the surface than that, but on average they are more than three and a half kilometres deep. Only about 2.5 percent of Earth's water is fresh.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-ESS2-2 has 5th graders describe and graph the amounts of salt and fresh water on Earth, and Florida's grade 5 lessons (SC.5.E.7.2) teach that the oceans contain 97 percent of it.

questions.question: Only a small part of Earth's water is fresh water, without the salt of the sea. Where is most of that fresh water?
choices: In ice caps and glaciers
In lakes, ponds and rivers
In the air, as water vapour
In swamps and marshes
questions.context: About 69 percent of Earth's fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers, and about 30 percent is underground as groundwater. Lakes and rivers, where fresh water is easiest to see, hold only a tiny fraction of it, and so do swamps and the air.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-ESS2-2's core idea teaches 5th graders that most fresh water is in glaciers or underground, with only a tiny fraction in streams, lakes, wetlands and the air.
